yt_text_polls.hook: Crypto Twitter feels unusually divided about September, so let us settle it.
yt_text_polls.question_text:
Crypto Twitter feels unusually divided about September, so let us settle it here.

The bear case is real: the Fed meets on the 16th and the market is pricing better than a coin flip on a rate HIKE, not a cut. That is the kind of print that shakes people out.

The bull case is the calendar right behind it. There is a wall of buyers waiting for a dip that keeps not arriving, the Clarity Act gets its cloture vote on the 15th, and hot money is already rotating out of AI and back into crypto.

My own base case is that we tag lower first and October is bullish almost no matter what happens in September, because everybody is queued up to buy that candle.

Where do you actually stand?
options: Bearish September, we tag lower first
Chop, and October is the real move

yt_text_polls.topic: Which dog actually gets listed on the Robinhood app
yt_text_polls.hook: Robinhood posted about dogs and Crypto Twitter decided that confirms a listing.
yt_text_polls.question_text:
Robinhood posted about dogs, asked people to show the goodest one they know, and Crypto Twitter decided that confirms Good in the Hood is getting listed on the app.

I do not buy it. Goodest is just how Americans talk to dogs; who is the goodest boy. I think whoever wrote that post was thinking about cute dogs, not a ticker.

And the numbers make the order look strange. Good in the Hood is around 8 million and paired to wrapped ETH. Artificial Inu is around 184 million, paired to tokenized NVDA, and that NVDA pool holds roughly three times the liquidity of its ETH pool. Cash Cat is the king of the whole chain and it is not even a coincidence: Cash Cat was Robinhood's original working name under Vlad Tenev and Baiju Bhatt, mascot and all.

So if one of them actually gets listed on the app, which one is it?
options: Good in the Hood, the rumor is right
Artificial Inu, the numbers decide it
Cash Cat, it was the original name

yt_posts.topic: On the Robinhood chain the listing is the catalyst, and it is not diligence
yt_posts.body_style: receipt-first: the listing timeline carries the whole argument
yt_posts.engagement_question: Would you buy a coin called Chump at 37 million, or is that exactly where you draw the line?
yt_posts.body:
Tendies got listed on Crypto.com and printed a brand new all time high the same day. Around 37 million at the top, up 70 percent before it started giving some back.

None of my alerts fired on it. I never hooked Tendies into the system, so there was nothing to fire. That gets fixed tonight.

But here is the part that should bother you more than the alert did.

The same week, a coin called Chump got its listings too. Not a product. Not a team you have heard of. A coin called Chump.

Chump launched on July 31st at a market cap of about 2,230 dollars. It just printed a fresh all time high and it is sitting near 37 million. That is better than a 16,000x in about a month.

So what changed in that month? Not the product, because there isn't one. CoinMarketCap on August 21st. LBank on August 29th. A brand new all time high today. Listings. That is the entire delta.

This is the thing I keep saying and people keep arguing with me about. On this chain the listing is not a milestone that follows the value. The listing IS the value. Insiders plus funding plus a centralized exchange equals a nine figure ambition on a coin whose whole concept is a rhyme with Trump.

Now the other side of it, because this cuts both ways and it will cut you.

Longbow built a real looking website at longbow.cash, a real looking company, an X profile with just enough history to survive a glance. They got their leg up. Then they rugged everybody.

A month later the same dev is back at longbow.credit. Same logo. Different color. It is listed on Ourbit and it is pumping again right now.

That is the pattern, and it is not rare. Fake company, fake history, sometimes a real exchange listing, one leg up, gone. A centralized exchange listing does not prove a project is safe. It proves somebody had the money and the contacts to buy one.

So use listings as the catalyst, never as the diligence. Check whether the X button on the profile goes to an actual account instead of a single post. Check whether they publish content or just publish promises. And check the market cap against the candles before you size in, because DexScreener has been serving stale numbers this week and it will hand you an entry that does not exist.

Would you buy a coin called Chump at 37 million, or is that exactly where you draw the line?

carousel_version_note: yt-post-2026-09-03-listings-are-the-cheat-code -> VERSION 4 (hook photo + data). Chosen on the post's own content, and it is the clear fit rather than a forced one: the argument IS a dated number series (launch cap $2,230 on Jul 31, CoinMarketCap Aug 21, LBank Aug 29, all time high Sep 1, ~$29.3M today, better than 6,700x), and V4 is the only version whose three stat boxes plus centre chart plus warning box can carry three separate quantitative beats per slide. V1 (news flash) would have shouted the hook but thrown the timeline away, and V2 (editorial) has one insight line and one content box, which cannot hold a three date listing sequence. The hook slide also has a genuine topic photo available, which is V4's actual precondition: schedule-tweets/images/reference/tendies.jpg supplies the subject and the green on black color world, attached as the SECOND ref alongside the mandatory version4/hook.png style exemplar. Slides 2 to 5 anchor on version4/slide.png. Extra weight to V4 per the run instruction, and it did not have to be forced. CAVEATS: (1) V4 chart lines are illustrated, not plotted from real data. Every STAT BOX value and every date is real and verified against CoinMarketCap and CoinGecko; the chart SHAPES are approximations of those moves. (2) The version4/slide.png exemplar itself contains em dashes and an @cryptodaily watermark, so every data slide prompt explicitly forbids both; check both at visual QA. (3) The tendies.jpg reference is banner art carrying a baked TENDIES wordmark, so the hook prompt states it is a subject and color key only and that its lettering must not be reproduced; sweep all four corners at boosted brightness during QA.
